title: Build vector clocks that catch a double-sold seat
prompt:
Two replicas of the ticket site, VA (Virginia) and OR (Oregon), both store who holds seat 14C. During a network partition each one accepts a write. Timestamps cannot tell you which write is "newer" (clocks drift), but vector clocks can tell you something more useful: whether one write had seen the other, or whether they were concurrent (a real conflict a human or a rule must resolve).

A clock is a plain object like { VA: 2, OR: 1 }. A missing node counts as 0. Implement:

  • tick(clock, nodeId) (done for you) returns a new clock with that node's counter + 1.
  • merge(a, b) returns a new clock with the per-node maximum.
  • compare(a, b) returns 'before', 'after', 'equal' or 'concurrent'.
  • class Replica with write(value), receive(version), read(). A replica keeps a list of versions { value, clock }. More than one version means conflicting siblings.
    • write: new clock = merge of all held clocks, then tick own id; replaces all held versions; returns { value, clock }.
    • receive: if the incoming clock is before or equal to any held version, ignore it (stale or duplicate) and return false. Otherwise drop held versions that are before it, add it, return true.
    • read: the values of all held versions.
compare({ VA: 1 }, { VA: 2, OR: 1 })        // 'before'
compare({ VA: 2, OR: 1 }, { VA: 1, OR: 2 }) // 'concurrent'

const va = new Replica('VA'), or = new Replica('OR');
const a = va.write('Alice');   // { VA: 1 }
const b = or.write('Bob');     // { OR: 1 }  (partitioned: never saw Alice)
va.receive(b); va.read();      // ['Alice', 'Bob']  conflict detected

tests.name: tick and merge return new clocks (no mutation)
compare: before, after and equal (missing node = 0)
compare: concurrent writes are detected
tests.code:
assertEqual(compare({ VA: 2, OR: 1 }, { VA: 1, OR: 2 }), 'concurrent');
assertEqual(compare({ VA: 1 }, { OR: 1 }), 'concurrent');

tests.name: a newer version replaces the older one; a late, stale copy is ignored
a duplicate delivery is ignored
partition: concurrent writes on both sides become siblings
a write after reading the siblings resolves the conflict everywhere

hints: merge: start from a copy of a, then for every entry of b keep the larger number. compare: walk the union of both key sets and record two booleans, "a is bigger somewhere" and "b is bigger somewhere".
Both booleans true means concurrent. Only aBigger means after; only bBigger means before; neither means equal. In write, fold every held clock together with merge before calling tick.

receive shape:

for (const v of this.versions) {
  const c = compare(incoming.clock, v.clock);
  if (c === 'before' || c === 'equal') return false;
}
this.versions = this.versions.filter(v => compare(v.clock, incoming.clock) !== 'before');
this.versions.push({ ...incoming });
return true;
explain:
This is how Amazon's original Dynamo and Riak detect conflicts: each object carries a version vector, replicas keep concurrent versions as siblings, and the next writer (or a merge rule) resolves them. Vector clocks never pick a winner on their own; they tell you honestly when there is no winner. Note the cost: one counter per node that ever wrote, so real systems prune or use dotted version vectors.

Say it in the interview: "Wall-clock last-write-wins can silently drop a write because clocks drift. If concurrent updates matter, I'd use version vectors to detect them and resolve with a domain rule. For something like seat inventory I'd avoid the conflict entirely with a single leader or consensus-backed store, because a detected double sale is still a double sale."
